title: Extension of coherence time beyond breakeven point using only drives and dissipation
summary: Quantum error correction aims to mitigate the loss of quantum information to the environment and is a central requirement for scalable quantum computing. Existing implementations are mainly based on measurement-based feedback, but constraints on read-out fidelity, hardware latency and system complexity can limit performance and scalability. Autonomous quantum error correction offers a complementary route based on engineered drives and dissipation, without repeated measurements or classical feedback. Here we implement an autonomous quantum error correction protocol, derived from quantum channel simulation, that repeatedly restores a photon-loss-corrupted logical qubit by transferring error information to ancilla qubits and resetting them. Unlike earlier demonstrations based on manifold stabilization through code-specific Hamiltonian and dissipation engineering, our approach is, in principle, applicable to arbitrary recovery maps. Using a binomial code encoded in a long-lived bosonic mode, we extend the logical qubit coherence time to 1.04 times that of the best physical qubit in the system. This result shows that drives and dissipation can extend the coherence time of an error-corrected bosonic logical qubit beyond the breakeven point. An autonomous quantum error correction protocol based on engineered drives and dissipation extends the coherence time of a bosonic logical qubit beyond that of the best physical qubit in the same system.

title: Extending qubit lifetime beyond break-even and enhancing quantum sensing by autonomous quantum error correction
summary: Extending the lifetime of a logical quantum bit (qubit) beyond that of the best physical qubit available within the same system—the break-even point—is a prerequisite for building practical quantum computers. Previous demonstrations have crossed this threshold using active quantum error correction (QEC), which measures an error syndrome and then applies an adaptive correction. Reaching the break-even point with autonomous QEC, which removes the need for resource-intensive measurement and feedback, remains challenging. Here we demonstrate beyond-break-even autonomous error correction in a circuit quantum electrodynamics system. We encode a photonic logical qubit in a superconducting microwave cavity and protect it against photon loss using engineered dissipation. The protected logical qubit achieves a lifetime of about 2.0 ms, 18% longer than that of the best physical qubit available in the system. We then use the protocol to measure a small frequency shift, obtaining a metrological gain of 6.3 dB relative to the most robust Fock-state superposition. These results show that autonomous QEC not only represents a necessary step towards fault-tolerant quantum computation but also offers advantages for robust quantum sensing. A measurement-free quantum error-correction protocol is shown to extend the lifetime of a bosonic logical qubit beyond the best physical qubit in the same system. This also offers prospects for enhanced quantum sensing.

title: Optimal learning of quantum channels in diamond distance
summary: The evolution of quantum states can be described by quantum channels. The task of estimating an unknown quantum channel, known as process tomography, is a central problem in quantum information theory. A long-standing open question is how many uses of an unknown channel are required to learn it to a precision quantified by the standard metric for distinguishing quantum processes, known as the diamond distance. Here we address this by establishing the query complexity of channel tomography with optimal dependence on the dimensions of the input and output spaces and the channel’s Kraus rank at any fixed constant accuracy in diamond distance. We design an algorithm that establishes an upper bound and prove a matching lower bound for learning a channel to the given accuracy. Our algorithm follows the strategy of performing optimal tomography on the Choi-state representation of the process, and we show that channel tomography can be reduced to the well-studied problem of pure-state tomography. As channels subsume states, unitaries and measurements as special cases, our protocol provides a unified framework for tomography of these tasks. Quantum channels can be used to describe the evolution of quantum states, including both unitary evolution and measurement. Now the optimal number of uses needed to learn an unknown channel to any fixed accuracy has been found.

title: Bound states in the continuum through quantum interference in ultracold atomic collisions
summary: Quantum-mechanical interaction potentials support localized bound states below the dissociation threshold or delocalized scattering states above it. Although bound states are energetically isolated, scattering states couple a quantum system to environmental modes, making dissipation and loss intrinsic to open systems. Bound states in the continuum are an exception, as destructive interference keeps them localized within the scattering continuum. Theory predicts that such states can arise through interference between two Feshbach resonances coupled to a common continuum. Here we form such an interference-stabilized state in ultracold collisions of 6Li atoms by coherently coupling two tunable Feshbach resonances using Floquet engineering. At a critical parameter point, elastic and inelastic coupling to the continuum vanish, producing a molecular state above the dissociation threshold. Consequently, resonant scattering features disappear and the colliding atoms become effectively transparent to one another. Full coupled-channel calculations and a minimal non-Hermitian model quantitatively reproduce our observations and identify the state as a Friedrich–Wintgen bound state in the continuum. These results show how quantum interference can control openness in quantum matter and enable the engineering of non-Hermitian Hamiltonians. Resonances in ultracold collisions couple to scattering states, causing interactions and loss. Now it is shown that the interference of Feshbach resonances creates a bound state in the continuum that decouples from elastic and inelastic scattering.

title: The cost of easy answers
summary: In leading the workshop, we sought to remain open-minded, recognizing that no one knows where this technology will lead. AI offers clear benefits, from polishing prose and aiding non-native English speakers to accelerating drafting. The relative vagueness of AI guidelines issued by major journals such as Nature and Science reflects the prevailing uncertainty. But we also tried to emphasize the potential cognitive costs of reliance on AI, especially the atrophy of essential human skills. Learning and conceptual mastery require effort and struggle, and may suffer if the heavy lifting is farmed out to a machine. Shortly after the workshop, I came upon a paper in Nature Machine Intelligence by Irene Unceta, Paula Subías-Beltrán and Oriol Pujol, who frame the cost of using AI in a particularly useful way ( Nat. Mach. Intell . 8 , 1328–1330; 2026 ). Their thesis is that when individuals rely on generative AI to perform tasks without spending time and effort to understand the output, something important gets lost. A gap opens between what individuals present to the world and what they can reconstruct, defend or understand. The authors call this gap epistemic debt: a disconnection between work bearing our name and our understanding of it. title: Active-flow-driven DNA remodelling generates millimetre-scale mechanical oscillations
summary: DNA undergoes continuous and rhythmic mechanical remodelling through condensation, looping and disentangling to regulate gene expression, segregate chromosomes and guide morphogenesis. Here we demonstrate a purely mechanical route to rhythmic DNA reorganization in a minimal active composite of microtubules, kinesin motors and DNA. We embed DNA polymers in an active-turbulent microtubule–kinesin fluid, creating a self-morphing material. The active flows stretch and entangle the DNA, forming a self-organized viscoelastic network that resists active stresses and affects flow over large length scales. This mechanical feedback loop progressively amplifies velocity correlations and drives a sharp non-equilibrium transition tuned by DNA contour length: from disordered flow to synchronized, millimetre-scale oscillatory flow. We rationalize the sharp transition with an active-gel model that predicts a growing length scale and an oscillatory instability emerging from the interplay between activity, orientational order and self-generated viscoelasticity, rather than chemical signalling. The theoretical dependence of the oscillation frequency on system size and activity is in agreement with observations. Thus, flow-driven DNA remodelling provides a minimal physical route to autonomous, system-spanning oscillations in three dimensions and suggests design principles for programmable soft matter that coordinates, actuates and reshapes itself. Active matter can exhibit turbulent or coherent flows. Now it is shown that active flows can entangle DNA polymers, leading to a non-equilibrium transition from disordered turbulence to periodic motion.

title: Coherence enhancement through equilibration to near-zero optical temperatures
summary: The conservation of phase-space volume in Hamiltonian systems rules out a host of desirable processes across the physical sciences, forbidding the enhancement of radiance through linear and passive optical elements and purification of incoherent states through unitary transformations in isolated settings. Apparent violations are typically sought using gain media and active feedback. Here we introduce an entropic framework that harnesses a fully conservative mechanism, whereby nonlinearity reshapes phase space to relax a multimode system into a pure ground state, even when excited with strongly incoherent inputs. The resulting near-zero-temperature state exhibits minimal statistical fluctuations without the need for active phase alignment. We experimentally observe this behaviour in nonlinear photonic mesh lattices, where efficient spatial coherence enhancement manifests despite the irreversible maximization of entropy. The generality of the underlying mechanism amongst conservative weakly nonlinear multimode systems suggests broad applicability across disciplines, from high-brightness laser sources to controlled condensation in many-body quantum systems such as Bose–Einstein condensates. Phase-space conservation bars coherence enhancement in passive linear optics, a limit often bypassed by gain or feedback. Here conservative nonlinearity reshapes phase space, thermodynamically driving incoherent light towards a coherent equilibrium.

title: Recent progress in the computational study of supercooled and glassy water
summary: Computer simulation has become an essential tool for investigating the complex behaviour of cold, non-crystalline forms of water. In the past few years, improved computational capabilities, the use of advanced sampling algorithms and the rapid adoption of machine learning methods have driven major progress in the computational exploration of the properties of supercooled and glassy water. Here we review recent progress in this area, focusing on pure bulk water, and covering simulations of supercooled water using classical potentials, simulations of supercooled water using machine learning potentials and simulations of glassy water. The article selectively reviews work that, either methodologically or in its findings, has helped to define the current understanding of cold, disordered states of water that are metastable with respect to crystalline phases. This Review discusses recent advances in the computational exploration of the properties of supercooled and glassy water.

title: Thermodynamic demonstration of tetracriticality and multicomponent superconductivity in UTe 2
summary: The candidate topological superconductor UTe2 exhibits a complex phase diagram with multiple superconducting states, and the nature of their coexistence is not yet resolved. In particular, the apparent observation of two intersecting second-order phase boundaries at a triple point in the pressure–temperature phase diagram is thermodynamically forbidden. This suggests either a hidden phase transition or a fundamental misunderstanding of the superconductivity in this material. Here we observe an additional phase boundary that is characterized by an upward jump in the sound velocity. This is direct thermodynamic evidence for a phase transition in which superconducting order is lost on cooling. Our results establish a tetracritical point beyond which the ambient and pressure-induced superconducting order parameters form a multicomponent state. We use the measured phase diagram to demonstrate that strong competition between the two superconducting order parameters drives the loss of order when cooling, and leads to phase locking that suppresses superconducting fluctuations. These findings provide the definitive magnetic field–pressure–temperature phase diagram of UTe2 and establish a thermodynamic foundation for multicomponent superconductivity. Prior measurements of the phase diagram of UTe2 contain a triple point that is forbidden by thermodynamics. Now, an additional phase boundary is discovered that resolves this problem and confirms multicomponent superconductivity in this material.

title: Multiparticle quantum walks in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model
summary: A strong potential gradient can localize individual particles in a crystal or optical lattice by making ordinary hopping energetically costly. Interactions can nevertheless enable correlated hopping processes that preserve the system’s centre of mass or, equivalently, its dipole moment. This constraint gives rise to fractonic behaviour, in which isolated excitations are immobile but their bound states can move. Here we realize individual mobile bound states of fractons in a dipole-conserving Bose–Hubbard model and observe their coherent quantum dynamics. Starting from a one-dimensional chain of ultracold bosonic atoms in an optical lattice, we use site-resolved optical potentials to deterministically generate localized dipole and antidipole excitations, which represent mobile bound states of a hole and a doublon. We track their individual quantum walks and characterize their strongly interacting scattering dynamics. Our study provides a bottom-up investigation of a Hamiltonian with kinetic constraints and offers an approach to exploring low-energy phases of fractonic matter. Strong potential gradients can localize individual particles, but interactions can still generate collective motion. An experiment with ultracold atoms in a tilted lattice now shows this collective motion by tracking mobile bound states of fractons.

title: Motors use biased diffusion to shepherd diffusible proteins on microtubules
summary: Far-from-equilibrium mixtures of active and passive molecules self-organize, but the principles remain unclear. Microtubules are cytoskeletal polymers composed of 13 protofilaments bound by mixtures of actively moving motors and passively diffusing microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs). They can serve as a model system for self-organization on a multi-lane lattice. Here we show that motors can shepherd diffusive MAPs along the lattice by rectifying Brownian motion into net directional drift without motor–MAP binding. Our model reveals that biased movement increases when fewer protofilaments are accessible or when lateral diffusion between protofilaments is limited, and identifies local dimensionality and diffusion as key parameters governing spatial patterning. In particular, shepherding depends on the total number of motors bound to the microtubules, and not on the individual motor processivity. We experimentally recapitulate micrometre-scale shepherding with a kinesin-1 motor (K401) and a diffusive MAP (PRC1), which show no detectable binding. These findings suggest shepherding is an emergent mechanism by which ensembles of motors generate micrometre-scale spatial patterning and transport of MAPs without direct binding interactions. Microtubules are bound by active motors and passively diffusing proteins. Now it is shown that this mixture of active and passive molecules is a realization of rectified Brownian motion in active matter.

title: Automated inverse design of metainterfaces with tailored friction laws
summary: Providing dry solid contacts with on-demand macroscale frictional behaviour remains a formidable challenge in tribology, haptics and robotics. It has been shown that metainterfaces created from surfaces with engineered asperity-based topographies can achieve such friction control. However, only a few types of friction behaviour were demonstrated because suitable topographies were identified on the basis of human intuition. Here we introduce a numerical-optimization-based inverse design framework to automatically discover new metainterfaces that satisfy specified friction laws—relationships between friction and the normal force. To illustrate the framework’s versatility, we first expand the range of achievable friction coefficients for a given pair of materials. We next unlock friction laws showing power-law variation of frictional force with normal force, with exponents ranging between 2/3 and 1.35. We then achieve bilinear variation when the range of normal force is divided into segments, including cases for a smaller slope in the second segment than in the first. We validate relevant cases experimentally. Our automated framework enables systematic exploration of large parameter spaces, not limited to topography but potentially incorporating the individual asperities’ bulk material or surface physicochemistry. It offers design solutions for different friction laws and provides insights into the relationship between local interfacial properties and macroscopic friction. Understanding friction between contacting surfaces is important to improve device performance. Now a method is shown to discover materials that offer on-demand frictional behaviour using inverse design based on genetic algorithms.

title: Imaging hot-electron Thomson cooling beyond the Boltzmann–Onsager framework
summary: Classical Thomson cooling, constrained by lattice-dominated heat dissipation and the weak entropy variation of charge carriers under thermal equilibrium, remains inefficient within the Boltzmann–Onsager framework. Driving electrons far from equilibrium broadens their energy spectrum and smears the Fermi edge, and this amplifies the temperature dependence of the electronic entropy. However, the hot-electron thermoelectric response beyond the classical thermal equilibrium limit has remained unexplored due to the lack of direct access to hot-electron dynamics. Here we image spatial distributions of electron and lattice temperatures together with the corresponding thermoelectric signals in HgTe and HgCdTe nanoconstrictions using coupled scanning-probe techniques. In HgTe, weak electron–phonon coupling allows hot electrons to remain far from thermal equilibrium with the lattice, and this generates large electron temperature gradients and a pronounced Thomson compensation effect. In HgCdTe the response shifts towards lattice-mediated heat redistribution due to the suppressed non-equilibrium state. These observations reveal a pronounced departure from the conventional near-equilibrium Boltzmann–Onsager expectations in high-field thermoelectricity, identify the Thomson effect as a key channel of non-equilibrium energy dissipation and establish a platform for exploring non-equilibrium thermoelectric phenomena in nanoscale conductors. Classical Thomson cooling is inefficient. Now non-equilibrium energy dissipation with a breakdown of the Boltzmann–Onsager limit is demonstrated by imaging hot electrons in HgTe and HgCdTe quantum wells.

title: Three-dimensional cell morphology is mediated by curvature sensing and interfacial stress
summary: Curvature sensing of cells critically governs three-dimensional cell morphology, which is integral to tissue and organ development as well as the wound-healing processes. However, the underlying mechanism by which sensing occurs remains unclear. Here we investigate the physical principles that govern curvature sensing at both single-cell and monolayer levels. We find that the cell–substrate interfacial stress ratio—defined as the balance between the cell contractile stress and the cell–substrate adhesion stress—determines the two predominant three-dimensional cell morphology modes, namely, complete adhesion and partial interior detachment. When the interfacial stress ratio is much higher than unity, a rapid morphological shift from complete adhesion to partial interior detachment occurs. This process is irreversible, as it proceeds towards a lower-energy state. We observe this mode switching for various cell types, under pharmacological perturbations and across multicellular layers, offering a universal biophysical framework for regulating three-dimensional cell morphology. Cells adhering to micro-curved surfaces can exhibit either complete adhesion or partial interior detachment. This is now found to be determined by the balance between the cell contractile stress and the cell–substrate adhesion stress.

title: Particle collisions on a quantum computer
summary: Elementary particle physics rests on the discovery of particles produced in high-energy collider experiments. Now, a model collision above the threshold for particle production has been simulated on a quantum computer.

title: Maxwell’s demon with memory
summary: Maxwell’s demon may produce work using the information it obtains by measuring the system as fuel. Now, it is shown that the amount of produced work increases if the demon takes information about the dynamical correlations of the system into account.

title: Beating the break-even point with autonomous quantum error correction
summary: Quantum error correction protects fragile quantum information by encoding it in high-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Conventional protocols typically require repeated syndrome measurements, real-time feedback or post-selection, and multiple physical qubits, which add technical complexity. Here we realize autonomous quantum error correction with a logical qubit encoded in multiple internal spin states of a single trapped ion and surpass the break-even point for qubit lifetime. We use engineered spin–motion couplings to transfer error-induced entropy into motional modes, which is then dissipated by sympathetic cooling with an ancilla ion. This eliminates the need for measurement and feedback. By repeatedly applying this protocol, we observe lifetime extension under both ambient laboratory conditions and injected low-frequency magnetic noise. Our results show that the multilevel structure of trapped ions can support hardware-efficient quantum error correction and robust quantum memories with reduced overhead. Conventional quantum error correction requires repeated measurements and real-time feedback, which are technically complex. An autonomous implementation that eliminates these while beating the break-even point is demonstrated in a trapped-ion system.

title: 中国散裂中子源在锂电池高镍正极重构领域取得重要进展
summary: 中国科学院高能物理研究所东莞研究部殷雯研究员团队充分发挥中子束双重硬核能力——高能中子辐照实现材料体内无创结构重构，中子散射技术实现原子尺度微观结构精准“透视”解析，依托中国散裂中子源大气中子辐照谱仪（CSNS‑ANIS）和多物理谱仪（CSNS-MPI），对单晶高镍NCM正极开展原创性研究，该成果以“A High‑Nickel Cathode Material for Lithium‑Ion Batteries Integrating a Proposed 3D Ionic Percolation Network and Interwoven Layered/Rock‑Salt Nanodomains”为题发表于国际顶级期刊《J. Am. Chem. Soc.》。 高镍单晶正极材料能有效解决多晶材料易开裂、副反应严重的问题。但大尺寸单晶缺乏晶界，导致锂离子扩散路径过长，在深度脱锂时极易发生结构滑移，使材料陷入“高容量与高稳定性难以兼得”的瓶颈。常规改性方法往往局限于材料表面，难以深入颗粒内部破局。 高能中子不带电荷且穿透能力强，不同于离子束、电子束仅能作用于材料表层，快中子辐照能够深入单晶颗粒体相与晶格原子发生级联碰撞，殷雯团队应用CSNS-ANIS的高能快中子对单晶NCM颗粒进行辐照，并结合CSNS-MPI的中子粉末衍射（NPD）与对分布函数（nPDF）分析，精确捕捉到中子引发高镍正极长程Li/Ni反位无序及短程金属-氧八面体畸变。借助中子最大熵法（MEM），证实了辐照后材料晶胞内部锂离子迁移通道连通性显著增强。 这种中子“穿针引线”式的辐照重构，将原本致密的单晶内部诱发出丰富晶界与交织的“层状/岩盐”纳米畴。研究团队据此提出机制：晶界网络构建了“三维锂离子渗流网络”，如同为离子修建了立体快速通道；而交织的岩盐相纳米畴则充当“结构铆钉”，有效抑制不可逆相变。 得益于这一双功能架构，重构后的正极材料（NCM-N）实现了性能跃升：0.2C倍率下放电比容量高达213.9 mAh/g；即使在10C超高倍率下仍保持152.2 mAh/g；5C快充循环450圈后容量保持率高达80

title: Wigner crystals get dressed
summary: When repulsion overcomes their tendency to move freely, electrons can arrange into a crystal. Two experiments have now identified Wigner polarons, quasiparticles whose optical signatures reveal the collective response of the electron lattice.

title: Teleportation transition of surface codes on a superconducting quantum processor
summary: The surface code is a leading candidate for harnessing long-range entanglement to protect logical quantum information against errors, and teleportation of the code’s logical states is desirable for robust quantum information processing. However, large numbers of physical qubits are needed to produce well-protected logical states, making quantum teleportation a formidable experimental challenge. Here we demonstrate the teleportation of surface code states with code distances up to 7, implemented on a superconducting quantum processor with 125 qubits. We obtain a phase diagram for successful teleportation of the logical state by tuning the local entangling gates uniformly across a finite threshold. Furthermore, we show that the entangling threshold can be boosted by coherent qubit rotations that inject non-classical magic resources, restoring the duality symmetry of the surface code’s topological phase. This serves as a guiding principle to minimize the entanglement needed to achieve many-body teleportation. Our results establish the potential for surface code teleportation to enable distributed fault-tolerant quantum computation. Quantum teleportation is often discussed for individual quantum systems, but fault-tolerant quantum computers will encode information in multiqubit states. Now teleportation of surface code logical states has been demonstrated.

title: Superconductivity and ferroelectric orbital magnetism in semimetallic rhombohedral hexalayer graphene
summary: Rhombohedral multilayer graphene has become a platform for exploring correlated and topological quantum phases, enabled by its flat bands that carry Berry curvature. However, previous studies have mainly focused on separated conduction and valence bands. Here we study the semimetallic regime of rhombohedral hexalayer graphene in which the conduction and valence bands overlap. We reveal a rich phase diagram dominated by flavour-symmetry breaking, featuring correlated insulators, several pockets of superconductivity and two distinct multiferroic orbital magnetic orders. Near a band inversion, we observe two superconducting-like states confined to regions with coexisting electron and hole Fermi surfaces, suggesting a possible dual-carrier origin. Additionally, we identify a ferroelectric orbital magnetic state that undergoes sharp switching under unipolar electric fields, which signals spontaneous electric polarization. Unlike previously reported multiferroicity near zero electric field, this state exhibits magnetic hysteresis reversible by electric field, consistent with a phenomenological model of coupled electric and magnetic polarization. Our work elucidates the correlated semimetal regime in rhombohedral graphene and underscores its potential to host diverse quantum phases. The semimetallic regime in rhombohedral graphene has not been extensively explored. Now, correlated insulators, superconductivity and multiferroic orbital magnetic order are demonstrated in semimetallic rhombohedral hexalayer graphene.

title: Coherent phonon control beyond amplitude saturation in a sliding ferroelectric
summary: The breakdown of Hooke’s law marks the onset of nonlinear behaviour: when displacements become large, restoring forces weaken and Hookean proportionality fails. In quantum materials, intense optical excitation can drive the crystal lattice into a similar regime, where established linear relations between light, electrons and phonons no longer hold. Displacive excitation of coherent phonons, the principal mechanism for launching structural motion, typically assumes that lattice-driving forces scale linearly with the photo-excited carrier density. At high excitation, however, this linearity can break down, which fundamentally limits accessible lattice displacements. Here we show that such nonlinear limitations can be surpassed in a sliding ferroelectric by timing, rather than strengthening the optical drive. Time-resolved second-harmonic generation reveals that the interlayer-sliding phonon governing ferroelectricity saturates and even diminishes under single-pulse excitation. By means of first-principles calculations, we attribute this nonlinearity to band-specific electron–phonon coupling that induces competing forces on the lattice. By splitting the optical energy into two well-timed pulses that avoid populating counteracting states, we achieve markedly larger phonon amplitudes at fixed total fluence. The resulting enhanced sliding motion exposes a regime of anharmonic phonon coupling that emerges only far from equilibrium. Strong photoexcitation of phonons in a crystal can lead to a nonlinear response. Now it is shown that this breakdown of linearity can be overcome by the application of well-timed photoexcitation pulses in WTe2.

title: Light-induced asymmetric pseudogap below the critical temperature in cuprates
summary: High-temperature cuprate superconductors remain a key platform for studying the competition and coexistence of emergent quantum phases of matter. These include non-s-wave superconductivity with a high transition temperature, non-Fermi-liquid transport and the pseudogap regime. How superconductivity emerges alongside and competes with the pseudogap remains an open question. Here, by directly accessing the near-antinodal region of optimally doped Bi-based cuprates via time- and angle-resolved photoemission, we report a transient change from a symmetric superconducting-like density of states to an asymmetric pseudogap-like density of states when superconductivity is disrupted by a sufficiently high excitation fluence. We observe this change at electronic temperatures well below the equilibrium superconducting critical temperature. Conversely, when superconductivity is fully restored, the pseudogap is suppressed, as indicated by a particle–hole-symmetric density of states. We also observe the coexistence of pseudogap and superconducting features at intermediate times or intermediate fluence. Our findings challenge the view that superconductivity emerges from phase coherence in the pseudogap. Instead, we show that the two states compete and that the low-temperature ground state of cuprates reflects an interplay between the superconducting and pseudogap states. How superconductivity relates to the pseudogap in cuprates remains unclear. Now, time-resolved photoemission measurements show a light-induced pseudogap-like state below critical temperature, revealing a dynamic interplay with superconductivity.

title: Fibres and glasses are competing material states in protein condensation
summary: Dense, well-ordered material states of proteins form the amyloid fibres that are indicative of neurodegenerative disease in the brain. In addition to forming amyloid fibres, some of these proteins comprise condensates that are initially liquid-like but evolve to a glassy, solid-like phase. Fibre growth requires a large supply of monomers, and so it is often speculated that fibres emerge from within a dense condensate as it ages and its microscopic dynamics slow into a glassy state. Here we show that, in the model system Fused in Sarcoma (FUS), fibres grow overwhelmingly in the dilute phase surrounding the condensates; concurrently, the condensates evolve to a glassy arrested solid. The resulting protein fibres and glassy condensates are both distinct solid-like phases that coexist but do not directly interconvert. These findings suggest that there may be two competitive ageing pathways in FUS condensation that are linked through phase separation kinetics. Fibres are thought to emerge from a dense protein condensate ageing into a glassy state. It is now shown that protein fibres and glassy condensates may result from two competing ageing pathways.

title: A liquid-crystal analogue of the skyrmion Hall effect
summary: Topology provides a unifying framework across disciplines, ranging from particle physics and cosmology to condensed-matter systems. In condensed matter, one of its most striking manifestations is the skyrmion Hall effect, where skyrmions—emergent spin configurations characterized by a conserved topological charge—acquire a transverse velocity under driving. Recent advances have revealed that chiral liquid crystals host a wide variety of topological solitons, including torons and skyrmion tubes. Here we show that such solitons exhibit a Hall-like response under shear flow, undergoing a transverse drift away from the shear direction. Our theoretical analysis predicts a weak net transverse mass flow whose magnitude scales as the cube of the shear rate. However, tracer-particle experiments and numerical simulations show that the solitons do not behave as passive tracers of this flow: their transverse motion is much stronger, and in simulations, it occurs opposite to the net transverse mass current. A liquid-crystal analogue of the Thiele equation provides a simple physical framework that highlights the central role of flow vorticity in the effect. These results establish a liquid-crystal analogue of the skyrmion Hall effect and open pathways for microfluidic technologies that exploit soft topological solitons as functional building blocks. Magnetic skyrmions are known to exhibit a Hall effect in the presence of an electric current. Now it is shown that liquid-crystal solitons also exhibit a Hall-like drift under shear flow.

title: Evidence for spin-fluctuation-mediated superconductivity in electron-doped cuprates
summary: In conventional, phonon-mediated superconductors, the transition temperature and the linear-in-temperature normal-state scattering rate are linked through the electron–phonon coupling strength. In cuprate high-temperature superconductors, no equivalent relationship between critical temperature and electron–boson coupling has been identified. Here we highlight such a link with electrons scattering off commensurate antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations of variable strength. We use d.c. resistivity and high-field magnetoresistance to extract the scattering rate in electron-doped La2−xCexCuO4 as a function of doping. We reveal a highly anisotropic inelastic component to the scattering rate whose magnitude diminishes markedly as doping increases. The correlation we highlight between the strength of scattering and the critical temperature then identifies low-energy spin fluctuations as the primary pairing glue in electron-doped cuprates. The contrasting magnetotransport behaviour in hole-doped cuprates suggests that the higher critical temperature in those materials cannot be attributed solely to an increase in the coupling strength to the antiferromagnetic fluctuations. The success in modelling La2−xCexCuO4 reinforces the notion that resolving the origin of high-temperature superconductivity in hole-doped cuprates may require more than a simple extension of the Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory. The mechanism for superconductivity in cuprates is still not known. Now, the observation of a relationship between the critical temperature and strength of coupling between electrons and spin fluctuations suggests the latter as a prime candidate.

title: The extraction of work from hidden degrees of freedom
summary: Thermodynamics establishes that information acquired through measurement can be converted into work, as exemplified by Maxwell’s demon and Szilard engines. Most experimental realizations of information engines, however, implicitly assume Markovian environments, in which information exchanged with the surroundings is irreversibly lost. Many physical systems instead exhibit environmental memory, with hidden degrees of freedom retaining correlations with the history of the system and giving rise to non-Markovian dynamics. Whether and how such concealed memory can be harnessed as a thermodynamic resource has remained an open question. Here we experimentally demonstrate the extraction of work from environmental memory. Using time-resolved measurements on an optically trapped Brownian particle in equilibrium, we implement a time-delayed double-measurement protocol that retrieves information through backflow from hidden bath degrees of freedom. We show that this information backflow alters the relaxation dynamics, can be quantified independently of initial state effects and—when appropriately exploited—enhances work extraction. Notably, we identify regimes in which the extracted work exceeds the energy stored in the observable degree of freedom alone. Our results establish environmental memory as an experimentally accessible thermodynamic resource and reveal how non-Markovian dynamics can be systematically explored to improve the performance of information engines operating in time-correlated environments. According to the laws of thermodynamics, information can be converted into energy. An information engine that harnesses environmental memory and exhibits non-Markovian dynamics has now been realized in experiments.

title: Chaos control with broken symmetries
summary: By breaking both material and cavity symmetries, waves can be funnelled into robust closed-loop patterns. This dual-symmetry-breaking approach enables the development of a new class of devices for wave-based signal processing and sensing.

title: Cavity-less Brillouin strong coupling in a solid-state continuous system
summary: Strong coupling between two systems allows them to exchange coherent information before the systems decohere. This important regime in light–matter interactions has predominantly been reached in optical resonator configurations. Here we demonstrate strong coupling between optical and acoustic fields within a continuum of modes in a cavity-less configuration after a single pass through an optical waveguide. The underlying physical effect of anti-Stokes Brillouin–Mandelstam scattering in a highly nonlinear fibre at cryogenic temperature allows us to experimentally demonstrate strong coupling in a waveguide scenario. We show the splitting of the optoacoustic spectral response and introduce a technique to measure the avoided crossing of hybrid optoacoustic modes via forced detuning. This demonstration opens a path towards in-line acoustic-wave-based quantum signal processing in waveguide systems. Strong coupling between light and matter is typically realized in resonators. Now it is shown that this can happen in a cavity-less waveguide scenario in which the light passes through only once.

title: Reaction–diffusion competition drives anomalous relaxation of vitrimers
summary: Since their discovery in 2011, vitrimers—covalent associative network polymers—have challenged the traditional understanding of soft matter relaxation dynamics. Unlike typical glass-forming liquids, the viscous relaxation of vitrimers can be entirely decoupled from their underlying structural dynamics. In addition, the origin of the Arrhenius viscosity in vitrimers in the presence of super-Arrhenius structural relaxation behaviour has been of high interest due to its potential to provide readily reprocessable high-performance plastics. Here we identify two types of transient networks in the relaxation dynamics of vitrimers based on the ratio of atomic displacement scales required for bond exchange to those required to relax a segment. In systems where bond exchange requires only subsegmental motion, our results indicate that network relaxation is governed by a competition between chemical exchange reactions and segmental diffusion. This competition produces the signature network–segment decoupling of the vitrimers and also drives a commonly observed crossover between Arrhenius and super-Arrhenius behaviour. This suggests an explanation for long-standing puzzling features of vitrimer dynamics and establishes a foundation for rational vitrimer design. Vitrimers—polymers that form covalent networks—show glassy behaviour with viscosity decoupled from structural relaxation. This decoupling is now found to originate from a competition between chemical exchange reactions and diffusion processes.

title: Simultaneous high-fidelity single-qubit gates in a spin qubit array
summary: Silicon spin qubits offer a promising path to scalable quantum computing due to their compatibility with industrial semiconductor manufacturing. A key requirement for scaling quantum processors is the ability to perform high-fidelity operations in parallel across many qubits. However, simultaneous control remains a major challenge in silicon devices, as fidelities typically degrade under parallel operation. Here we identify microwave-drive-induced a.c.-Stark shifts as the dominant source of this degradation in a five-qubit silicon spin array. We address this by introducing a scalable mitigation protocol based solely on pairwise phase calibrations. Using tailored control pulses on a shared control line, we achieve primitive X and Y gate fidelities well above 99.99% for each qubit individually, with some approaching 99.999%. Furthermore, these fidelities are preserved above 99.99% during simultaneous operation of up to three qubits. During parallel five-qubit operation, fidelities remain above the widely targeted fault-tolerant threshold of 99.9%. By maintaining high-fidelity control during simultaneous operation, shared qubit-control lines can support the development of large-scale semiconductor quantum processors. Quantum computers require simultaneous control of multiple qubits, which is challenging to achieve in nanoscale semiconductor devices. Now high-fidelity parallel operations have been demonstrated for five silicon spin qubits.

title: Monolayer van der Waals kagome lattice for high-temperature flat-band physics
summary: Kagome lattice materials host a variety of intriguing quantum phenomena arising from the intrinsic interplay of topology, electron correlations and geometric frustration. Even though previous studies have primarily focused on bulk three-dimensional kagome materials, the realization of an ideal two-dimensional kagome system has remained a long-standing goal. Here we demonstrate ideal two-dimensional monolayer kagome lattices in the van der Waals material family A2T3X4, where A is an alkali metal, T is a transition metal and X is a chalcogen. Our nanofocused angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy directly characterizes the electronic structure of A2T3X4 down to the monolayer limit, revealing an isolated kagome-derived flat band just below the Fermi level. Through electrostatic gating, the kagome flat band can be further tuned to the Fermi level, enabling direct access to partially filled flat-band physics. Compared with existing moiré-based artificial flat-band systems, this monolayer kagome platform realizes more than 220-fold higher flat-band electron density, offering opportunities to explore emergent flat-band phenomena at temperatures higher than those currently achievable. The experimental realization of intrinsic 2D kagome materials with controllable flat bands has remained challenging. Now a van der Waals kagome material family is shown to host an isolated, gate-tunable flat band down to the monolayer limit.

title: 利用自旋关联探测强相互作用“色八重态”机制取得新进展
summary: 近日，中国科学院高能物理研究所岩斌副研究员团队与北京化工大学何志国教授在重夸克偶素的强相互作用机制研究中取得重要进展。研究团队首次提出，利用重夸克偶素衰变中末态粒子的自旋关联作为新的“物理指纹”，通过测量最终强子的角度分布可直接检验非相对论量子色动力学（NRQCD）中长期难以分离的“色八重态”机制，为精确检验NRQCD理论提供了新的实验途径。相关成果于9月25日发表在国际权威期刊《物理评论快报》（Phys. Rev. Lett. 137 (2026) 131903）。 重夸克偶素由重夸克和反夸克组成，是研究强相互作用的重要体系。由于重夸克质量较大，这类体系既能够进行较为精确的理论计算，又涉及复杂的非微效效应，因此长期以来一直是检验量子色动力学（QCD）的重要“实验室”。NRQCD是描述重夸克偶素产生和衰变的重要理论框架。其中重夸克对不仅可以处于“色单态”，还可以在中间过程中短暂处于“色八重态”组态。 “色”是夸克和胶子特有的一种量子属性，最终能够独立存在的强子整体必须是“无色”的，但其形成和衰变过程可以经历不同的颜色组态。色八重态并不是一种新的粒子，而是重夸克对演化过程中可能出现的重要中间量子状态。对于P波重夸克偶素，色八重态贡献是保证NRQCD因子化理论自洽不可或缺的一环。此外，色八重态还广泛参与 产生率和极化等关键观测的理论描述，因此准确确定其贡献，对于检验NRQCD理论及其普适性具有重要意义。 在底夸克偶素体系中，色八重态贡献仍存在明显不确定性。描述其贡献的相关非微扰参数中，格点理论计算与基于实验数据的唯象提取结果存在显著差异。因此，如何对色八重态机制进行更加独立和直接的实验检验，成为底夸克偶素研究中的重要问题。 传统研究主要依赖底夸克偶素的衰变率推断色单态和色八重态的贡献，但两种机制往往同时贡献到同一衰变过程，难以仅凭事件数量进行有效区分。研究团队发现，在底夸克偶素 衰变中，两种机制具有不同的末态自旋结构，其中色八重态会产生具有特定横向自旋关联的轻夸克对。该自旋信息可通过强子化转换为末态强子的特定方位角关联，从而使实验能够利用“自旋指纹”区分不同的强相互作用机制

title: Morphogenesis of a stratified cell mound at a vortex defect
summary: Topological defects in cell monolayers have been recognized as mechanical organizing centres in morphogenetic processes. However, the mechanism by which cells coordinate their motion at such defects and self-organize into higher order structures remains elusive. Here we describe the formation of three-dimensional multicellular mounds in unconfined myoblast monolayers at well-controlled vortex topological defects. Before the onset of the formation of a bilayer, the vortex structure induces millimetre-scale cell flows that converge towards the defect centre. As a result, three-dimensional cell mounds form at the defect core, layer by layer. These mounds grow by interlayer permeation sustained by the converging cell flows. At late stages, the bell shape of the structured mounds can be modelled with dynamics driven by these converging flows. Our results highlight the crucial role of integer topological defects in driving large-scale cell flows that result in the formation of highly ordered three-dimensional tissues from a monolayer. We propose that similar mechanisms may be at play in certain morphogenetic and tumorigenic events. In cell monolayers with a vortex-like orientation defect, cells converge towards the core of the defect and form a highly organized three-dimensional mound. This mechanism may be relevant for morphogenesis and tumorigenesis.

title: Chip-mediated manipulation of photonic quantum skyrmions
summary: Quantum skyrmions are attracting much interest owing to their topological robustness, which offers a route to address noise and loss in quantum systems. The toolkit for their creation has advanced recently, enabling quantum skyrmions to be generated in bulk systems as entangled states and on chip as single-photon states. However, methods for generating on-chip entangled skyrmions, as well as for their reconfigurable manipulation and controlled interfacing with single-photon skyrmions, remain elusive. Here we demonstrate entangled skyrmions and their manipulation on chip with an integrated silicon nitride nanophotonic platform. The skyrmion topology is coherently encoded in a local single-photon spin-textured quantum state, which is subsequently transferred into a non-local skyrmion topology shared between two entangled photons. Throughout the transfer process, the topology remains preserved under background noise and different types of disturbance, even after the entanglement vanishes. This establishes a quantum-topology-enabled transfer scheme beyond entanglement, which reveals a fundamentally enhanced resilience that outperforms conventional entanglement-assisted quantum state transfer. This approach serves as a step towards building robust quantum interconnects and advancing distributed quantum information technology mediated by topology. Although photonic quantum skyrmions can be generated as entangled or single-photon states, a means to switch between the two is required for quantum information processing. Now, entangled skyrmions and their manipulation on chip is realized.

title: Orthorhombic ice
summary: Ice X, which has been observed experimentally at extreme pressures and room temperature, is a symmetric hydrogen-bonded phase of water, in which oxygen atoms form a body-centred cubic lattice and hydrogen atoms occupy positions midway between neighbouring oxygen atoms. At still higher pressures, adjacent atomic layers are predicted to shear relative to one another. This distortion lowers the crystal symmetry from cubic to orthorhombic and gives rise to ice XXII. Verifying this transition has proved difficult because achieving such ultrahigh pressures and collecting reliable structural information from minute samples is technically challenging. To overcome these challenges, Osmond and colleagues performed static compression experiments using a diamond anvil cell and advanced synchrotron X-ray diffraction techniques with enhanced source brilliance and beam-focusing capabilities. The team conducted a series of static compression experiments and achieved pressures exceeding 300 GPa. Using high-resolution Raman spectroscopy, they monitored the evolution of the crystal lattice of ice X during compression. A phonon mode corresponding to oxygen vibrations within the symmetric hydrogen-bond network of ice X appeared above a threshold pressure. As pressure increased further, this mode progressively broadened and split into two distinct components, indicating a gradual lowering of crystal symmetry. At higher pressures, the signal was too weak to resolve, but extrapolating the measured trends gave results consistent with predictions for ice XXII. title: The old powers on
summary: There are, however, some inconvenient empirical facts. Notably, the contemporary world consumes more oil, more coal and more wood than at any other point in human history. Most people in England believe that the country uses negligible amounts of wood for heating or energy generation, assuming wood fires had faded into obscurity along with smoky Victorian hearths. Yet the Drax power station in North Yorkshire, originally constructed to burn coal, now operates primarily by burning millions of tonnes of imported wood. In 2021, the plant burned more wood than the current annual UK forestry production — four times as much as England did in the mid-eighteenth century. Energy transitions, it turns out, are not actually transitions. At least none of them so far. This is the central thesis of historian Jean-Baptiste Fressoz’s More and More and More (Penguin Books, 2025). Over time, humanity has brought an ever-expanding suite of energy sources into play, but these additions do not replace their predecessors. Instead, they act symbiotically, expanding industrial capacity and creating new mechanisms to extract, process and consume in an endless spiral of material accumulation. Fressoz systematically examines each alleged historical transition, documenting with economic and material data that the absolute consumption of earlier primary resources did not decline as new ones emerged. title: Order from chaos with adaptive circuits on quantum hardware
summary: Programmable quantum devices provide a platform for controlling the coherent dynamics of quantum wave functions. Monitoring and feedback can control classically chaotic dynamics, but extending these approaches to quantum systems is challenging because chaotic evolution amplifies perturbations and is sensitive to noise and decoherence. Here we demonstrate adaptive monitored quantum circuits that incorporate conditional feedback into non-unitary evolution, using local mid-circuit measurements and resets to control quantum chaotic dynamics. We perform the experiments on an IBM superconducting quantum processor with up to 100 qubits, implementing a quantum version of the classically chaotic Bernoulli map. The map scrambles quantum information, whereas local measurements and feedback attempt to steer the dynamics towards a fixed point of the map. This competition drives a dynamical phase transition between quantum and classical dynamics, which we observe experimentally and describe theoretically using noisy simulations, matrix product states and mappings to statistical mechanics models. By successfully applying up to nearly 5,000 entangling gates and 5,000 non-unitary mid-circuit operations on systems up to 100 qubits, the quantum processor yields accurate estimates of the universal critical properties. Controlling quantum chaos requires using measurement and feedback that survive noise and decoherence. Such control is now achieved in a superconducting quantum processor and reveals a critical transition between quantum and classical dynamics.

title: Lift from the flow
summary: The team created a hydrodynamic maze in a laboratory water channel using an array of jets. This produced alternating regions of fast, turbulent water and relatively calm flow. They then used a high-speed camera to record 20 giant danio ( Devario aequipinnatus , pictured) fish swimming through the maze with three different flow conditions. Calicchia and Ni observed that, as the jet speed increased, the fish became increasingly concentrated in the calmer spaces between the jets. A closer look at their movements revealed that, upon entering energetically costly regions, the fish turned their bodies at an angle with respect to the flow and moved sideways towards more favourable locations. By turning their bodies relative to the incoming flow current, fish can generate lift-like forces — the same type of force that acts on an aircraft wing. These forces may help carry the fish sideways across the flow. Calicchia and Ni further found that the fish maintained this angled orientation without a considerable increase in drag. title: Active wetting of an implanting embryo
summary: When a liquid droplet sits on a surface, the competition between the liquid’s surface tension and its adhesion to the substrate determines how much the liquid can spread. If the droplet instead consists of living, motile cells, such as an implanting embryo, additional active cellular forces affect wetting. In tissues, for example, the active wetting transition is governed by a competition between traction forces and contractile intercellular stresses. The team studied implantation biomechanics by analysing how mouse embryos attached and spread across a substrate (see image, which shows a schematic of this process). Embryos from aged mice displayed reduced spreading, which impaired implantation. Using active wetting theory, the team found that this spreading reduction was caused by higher actomyosin contractility, which increased the aged embryos’ surface tension and tissue viscosity. Pharmacological manipulation further confirmed the functional role of actomyosin contractility during implantation. title: Short-range excitonic correlations and enhanced excitonic susceptibility in 1 T -TiSe 2
summary: Excitons—bound states of electrons and holes—can spontaneously condense into a quantum coherent ground state. 1T-TiSe2, a layered transition metal dichalcogenide, is a candidate for realizing this phase in a bulk material, but its putative excitonic condensation is accompanied by charge-density-wave formation that obscures signatures of excitonic instability and fluctuations in this structural transition. Here we clarify the mechanism of exciton condensation in quasi-low-dimensional systems by tracking exciton dissociation as a function of photoexcitation fluence and temperature using few-femtosecond broadband extreme-ultraviolet absorption spectroscopy. We find that short-range excitonic fluctuations emerge before long-range-order formation in the ground state. We also observe enhanced excitonic susceptibility, identified by faster exciton dissociation near the phase transition temperature, consistent with excitonic instability in this material. These results provide a framework for understanding other excitonic insulator candidates proposed in quasi-one- or quasi-two-dimensional crystals. In bulk materials, excitonic condensation is hard to separate from charge-density-wave formation. Now short-range excitonic correlations are revealed above the transition temperature in 1T-TiSe2 via few-femtosecond extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy.

title: Picosecond current pulses probe intrinsic limit for dissipationless transport in superconductors
summary: Picosecond current pulses can propagate with zero resistance far above the conventionally defined critical current values in type-II superconductors. Such pulses have now revealed the onset of resistive transport at a higher current threshold in the s-wave superconductor NbN, associated with Cooper-pair depairing. By contrast, a gradual suppression of superconductivity is observed in YBa2Cu3O7, reflecting the d-wave nature of its superconducting state.

title: Non-reciprocity in quantum technologies
summary: Non-reciprocity—the ability to transmit signals in one direction while blocking them in the reverse—has become an important resource for quantum technologies, enabling directional amplification, routing of quantum information and topologically protected quantum states. Recent experimental advances have demonstrated non-reciprocal behaviour in low-loss, fully integrated devices operating with weak or no magnetic bias fields. Many of the most mature demonstrations so far have been realized in microwave-frequency and superconducting circuits, but progress continues in parallel in optical and nanophotonic systems. These achievements overcome the limitations of more traditional approaches that use stronger magnetic bias fields. This makes non-reciprocity compatible with superconducting circuits and scalable quantum photonic architectures, as well as an integral part of the next generation of modular quantum computers, distributed quantum networks and precision metrology. Here we highlight the key concepts for engineering non-reciprocity in quantum systems and describe how this functionality can be used for high-fidelity qubit readout, robust quantum state transfer and boosting the sensitivity of quantum sensors. Non-reciprocity in the quantum regime promises unidirectional transport and enhanced sensing, but traditional approaches hinder device integration. This Review highlights magnet-free routes for engineering non-reciprocity in quantum systems.

title: A long-sought phase in CuGeO 3 traces the full evolution of spin fractionalization
summary: Neutron spectroscopy measurements combined with tensor network simulations have placed the long-studied quantum spin-chain compound CuGeO3 in a spontaneously dimerized phase predicted in 1982. In this system, fractionalized excitations evolve from nearly free spinons to tightly bound triplons across energy scales within a single spectrum.

title: Topological transitions in orbital-symmetry-controlled chemical reactions
summary: Tools that classify energy-level connectivity through topological invariants have become a standard in condensed-matter physics. More recently, the extension of these concepts to molecular systems has attracted substantial interest. Reactions governed by orbital symmetry conservation are ideal model systems to develop this extension, as they classify reaction pathways as symmetry allowed or symmetry forbidden depending on whether molecular-orbital energies cross along the reaction coordinate. However, the presence of strong electronic correlations in these reactions invalidates the framework underlying topological band theory, preventing a straight generalization. Here we introduce a formalism in terms of Green’s functions to classify reactions controlled by orbital symmetry even in the presence of strong electronic correlations. We show that symmetry-forbidden pathways are characterized by crossings of zeros in Green’s function, in contrast to the crossing of poles as predicted by molecular-orbital theory. We introduce symmetry-resolved invariants that provide end-point diagnostics for symmetry-preserving paths and discuss the direct tracking of zeros when the symmetry is weakly broken. The result is a many-body generalization of orbital-crossing selection rules and a bridge to established concepts from topological and strong interaction physics in a molecular setting. The application of ideas from topological band theory to reaction pathways in molecular systems with strong electronic interactions is challenging. Now, a many-body framework based on Green’s functions is introduced to solve this problem.

title: Reactions become topological

summary: 9 月 28 日，中国科学院档案馆组织档案专家组对国家重大科技基础设施——强流重离子加速器装置（ HIAF ）项目，开展了档案专项验收工作。专家组由来自中国科学院档案馆、科研院所的 7 位专家组成，中国科学院科技基础能力局和近代物理研究所相关部门共 40 余人参会。 档案验收专业组听取了项目建设情况及档案管理工作报告，就报告内容进行质询，现场抽查项目档案，审阅相关材料。 档案专家组认为，建设单位高度重视项目档案工作，工作网络健全，职责明确，同步管理机制完善，全过程业务指导和关键节点检查落实到位，做到了同部署、同实施、同验收。建设单位结合实际制定了项目文件材料归档范围，并将归档要求纳入合同、协议，保障了项目文件材料收集齐全、真实有效。项目档案质量、安全防护设施、保管条件符合国家和中国科学院有关规范要求。项目依托数字档案室开展了工艺设备安装总图、装置的 BIM 模型、科学数据等科研电子文件的收集整理，在国家重大科技基础设施档案信息化建设方面进行了有效探索。一致同意“强流重离子加速器装置项目”档案通过档案专业验收。 图 1 ：验收会议现场 图 2 ：参会人员合影 图 3 ：档案专家现场查阅档案实体 （科技处 供稿）

title: Towards foundation-style models for energy-frontier heterogeneous neutrino detectors via self-supervised pretraining
summary: Accelerator-based neutrino physics is entering an energy-frontier regime in which interactions reach the tera-electronvolt scale and produce exceptionally dense, overlapping detector signatures. Event interpretation is impractical for conventional reconstruction and challenging for supervised models trained from scratch, particularly when labelled data are scarce and analyses span diverse objectives. Here we present a sparse Vision Transformer framework for learning reusable representations from heterogeneous detector data. Self-supervised pretraining combines masked-autoencoder reconstruction with relational voxel-level objectives for hierarchy, ghost and particle identification, followed by joint fine-tuning across classification and regression tasks. On simulated events from the proposed FASER calorimeter (FASERCAL) concept, pretraining improves neutrino-flavour and charm-quark identification, momentum regression and vertex reconstruction, with relational objectives providing further gains in topologically complex channels. Attribution and representation diagnostics show a more structured latent space, while detector-subsystem ablations recover physically plausible channel-dependent roles. With roughly 103 labelled events, the pretrained encoder matches the flavour-classification performance of scratch training with an order of magnitude more data. Cross-domain transfer is observed on public plastic-scintillator and liquid-argon benchmarks. A matched alternative-generator stress test shows stable flavour and kinematic performance while exposing charm tagging as generator sensitive. title: Fully developed active turbulence defined through a non-equilibrium phase transition
summary: Non-equilibrium systems challenge the standard definitions of phases and phase transitions from equilibrium statistical physics. For example, in active fluids, continuous energy injection at the microscale drives the system intrinsically out of equilibrium. This process gives rise to collective turbulent-like flows whose onset remains poorly defined. Here we show that the onset corresponds to an activity-driven phase transition, marked by the emergence of a system-spanning critical backbone of vorticity nodal lines. Combining two independent experiments, namely, microtubule–kinesin active nematics and dense suspensions of swimming bacteria, with large-scale simulations of active nematics and fluctuating nematohydrodynamics, we show that this transition occurs at a critical activity threshold. Below this threshold, vorticity structures are fragmented and vortex centres form only finite, mechanically floppy networks. Above this threshold, the nodal lines of the vorticity field percolate and the vortex centres form a rigid, system-spanning cluster. The geometric transition is characterized by the emergence of critical percolation statistics for the vorticity nodal lines, whereas the mechanical transition reflects the emergence of a vortex configuration that shows rigidity percolation statistics for vortex centres. We show that both transitions are absent in equilibrium systems that obey detailed balance, demonstrating that the transition is intrinsically non-equilibrium. These results establish an experimentally accessible definition of fully developed active turbulence, linking microscopic activity to macroscopic geometry, and mechanics of living systems. title: Deterministic and programmable fusion for the scalable generation of photonic graph states
summary: Entanglement in multiphoton graph states is an important resource for applications such as measurement-based quantum computing and memoryless quantum repeaters. However, most experimental demonstrations have only successfully prepared small-scale instances. A method known as fusion provides a divide-and-conquer approach that can link smaller resource states into larger, more complex graphs. Its practical scalability in linear optical systems has been limited by the probabilistic nature of conventional fusion protocols, which necessitates extensive hardware overhead and feed-forward resources to achieve deterministic outcomes. Here we introduce and experimentally demonstrate a deterministic fusion operation on a superconducting circuit device with built-in error mitigation. Our scheme can connect small time-bin-encoded cluster states that are generated on demand into larger, reconfigurable photonic graph states of increased size. We implement fusion by non-destructively projecting pairs of flying microwave photons into Bell states. The protocol involves the active reset and reuse of superconducting qubits to circumvent the effects of decoherence. We demonstrate genuine multipartite entanglement across 13 photonic qubits, establishing a scalable framework for photonic graph-state synthesis. Graph states entangle many photons in a special structure that is useful for several quantum protocols. Making graph states is often probabilistic and inefficient, but now a deterministic approach using superconducting qubits has been demonstrated.

title: Multiscale transitional flow in anisotropic nanoparticle suspensions revealed by time-resolved X-ray scatter microscopy
summary: Complex fluids transition from laminar to transitional flow above a critical control parameter, in a similar manner to their Newtonian counterparts. In a continuum mechanics sense, fluid elements follow the ensuing complex trajectories, which gives rise to secondary flows in terms of macroscopic vortices. However, it is not known whether their trajectories exhibit the same spatiotemporal behaviour as the macroscopic flow field if idealized fluid elements are replaced with actual anisotropic nanoparticles. Here, to address this fundamental question, we develop a multiscale method that combines small-angle X-ray scatter microscopy with polarized light imaging, thereby bridging seven orders of magnitude in length scales. We demonstrate proof of principle for Taylor–Couette flow—a classical transitional flow problem—of platelet-like graphene oxide nanoparticle and rod-like cellulose nanocrystal suspensions. The analysis shows markedly different multiscale dynamics underlying flow stability: whereas the platelet-like particles follow the macroscopic dynamics of the secondary flows, as expected for high rotational Péclet numbers, the rod-like particles exhibit characteristic high-frequency orientational motion at moderate rotational Péclet numbers that correlates with the turnover frequency of the vortex instabilities. The trajectories of embedded particles provide a route for probing fluid flow dynamics. An X-ray scatter microscopy approach that enables precise monitoring of non-sphericalnanoparticles now reveals multiscale dynamics in complex fluids.

title: Hyperbolic wave attractors
summary: Wave behaviour in irregular cavities is typically dominated by chaos, whose diverging trajectories are highly sensitive to initial conditions due to complex internal reflections, and this limits control and stability. Here we show that odd-shaped cavities formed in hyperbolic media suppress chaotic wave dynamics and instead give rise to hyperbolic wave attractors: robust, chiral, broadband and scale-invariant states that organize wave motion analogously to limit cycles in nonlinear dynamical systems. Their defining properties differ from both conventional resonant cavities and chaotic modes. We experimentally demonstrate this phenomenon using elastodynamic waves in a hyperbolic metamaterial and reveal attractor phase transitions, symmetry-driven features and robustness against defects. These results show that wave-attractor physics extends across natural and artificial hyperbolic media and reveal how simultaneous symmetry breaking in the material and cavity geometry produces robust, chiral wave organization in a fully linear system. This work opens possibilities for compact, multifunctional devices in wave-based signal processing and sensing systems by merging functionalities traditionally associated with large, wavelength-scale structures with those of deeply subwavelength cavities. Wave propagation in irregular cavities made from conventional isotropic media is typically chaotic. Now odd-shaped cavities made from hyperbolic metamaterials are shown to suppress chaotic wave dynamics and produce stable geometric wave patterns.

title: Universal scaling laws for correlated decay of many-body quantum systems
summary: Quantum systems are inevitably open, continually exchanging energy and information with the surrounding environment. This interaction leads to decoherence and decay of quantum states. In complex systems, formed by many particles, decay can become correlated and enhanced. A fundamental question then arises: what is the maximal decay rate of a large quantum system, and how does it scale with its size? Computing this rate exactly is as hard as finding the ground-state energy of a generic spin Hamiltonian—a notoriously intractable problem. Here we exploit this correspondence to establish rigorous and general upper and lower bounds on the maximal decay rate. These bounds are universal, as they hold for a broad class of Markovian many-body quantum systems. For many physically relevant systems, the bounds are asymptotically tight, resulting in exact scaling laws with system size. Specifically, for large atomic arrays in free space, these scalings depend only on the dimensionality of the array and are insensitive to details at short length scales. The scaling laws set fundamental limits on the decay rates of all quantum states, shed light on the behaviour of generic driven-dissipative systems, and may ultimately constrain the scalability of quantum processors and simulators based on atomic arrays. Decoherence and decay of quantum systems arise from interactions with their environment that can be highly complex. Despite this complexity, bounds on the decay rate are found that are asymptotically tight in several important cases.

title: Quantum field theory dynamics on a spin–phonon quantum computer
summary: Simulating the non-equilibrium dynamics of quantum field theories in nature is generally intractable with classical methods, but is a promising application for quantum computers. Unfortunately, simulating interacting bosonic fields using quantum computers typically requires a boson-to-qubit encoding that can be resource-intensive. Furthermore, these encodings necessarily involve a truncation of the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space, introducing errors that grow with energy and time. Here we adopt an alternative approach that combines a qubit-based quantum computer with an active bosonic register that offers qubit, bosonic and mixed qubit–boson quantum gates. We use a hybrid analogue–digital trapped-ion quantum computer in which qubits are encoded in the internal states of the ions as well as the bosons in the ions’ motional states. Specifically, we simulate the non-equilibrium dynamics of a (1 + 1)-dimensional Yukawa model, a simplified model of interacting nucleons and pions. These dynamics populate high-bosonic-field excitations starting from an empty state, and the experimental results effectively capture such high-occupation states. By removing the need for a large qubit overhead and avoiding truncation errors, our simulation approaches the regime in which classical methods become challenging. Many physical systems involve bosons, which are resource-intensive to simulate with a qubit-based quantum computer. Now a hybrid approach that combines qubits and bosons has been used to simulate a quantum field theory of fermions and bosons.

title: Quantum field theory dynamics in trapped ions
summary: Computing the real-time dynamics of quantum field theories is intractable for classical devices. Now, the dynamics of two quantum field theories have been observed using hybrid trapped-ion quantum simulators.

title: Aharonov–Bohm interference in a $${\pmb{\mathbb{Z}}}_{\bf{2}}$$ Z 2 lattice gauge theory on a hybrid qubit–oscillator quantum computer
summary: Lattice gauge theories, which have both dynamical matter and gauge fields, are strongly coupled problems that lie beyond the reach of classical computation. Quantum simulations may provide a tractable approach for studying lattice gauge theories, but implementing gauge-invariant encodings and real-time evolution remains experimentally challenging. Here we demonstrate a resource-efficient encoding of a $${{\mathbb{Z}}}_{2}$$ lattice gauge theory using a hybrid qubit–oscillator trapped-ion quantum device, with the qubits representing the gauge fields and the vibrational modes of the ions encoding the bosonic matter fields. We use synthetic dimensions to construct higher dimensional lattice geometries, and we combine digital and analogue techniques to prepare the initial states, realize the gauge-invariant real-time evolution and measure the relevant observables. After observing dynamics obeying Gauss’s law in a $${{\mathbb{Z}}}_{2}$$ link, we extend this approach to a loop geometry formed by two qubits and two oscillators. In this quasi-two-dimensional set-up, we observe Aharonov–Bohm interference with dynamical gauge fields encoding the magnetic flux, thereby demonstrating the interplay between charge and flux. Our results establish a path for scalable quantum simulations of lattice gauge theories in higher dimensions. Lattice gauge theories are difficult to study using classical computational methods. A dynamic quantum simulation of a lattice gauge theory on a two-site loop has now been demonstrated using a hybrid qubit–oscillator trapped-ion quantum computer.

title: A universal speed limit for collective decay in quantum systems
summary: Quantum systems composed of many particles can decay much faster than the sum of their individual decay rates. Now, a universal speed limit of many-body decay has been revealed, providing bounds on applications that rely on collective emission and a potential constraint on the scalability of quantum technologies.

title: Strange metal behaviour from underlying bad metallicity
summary: Metals that host strong electronic interactions, including high-temperature superconductors, behave in ways that do not conform to the conventional Fermi liquid theory. The microscopic origin of this so-called strange metal behaviour has not yet been clarified. Here we show that within the two-dimensional t–J model, strange metallicity is pervasive in the temperature-doping phase diagram whenever antiferromagnetic order is suppressed. We do this by examining the d.c. and frequency-dependent conductivity within this model, taking advantage of recent improvements made on the finite-temperature Lanczos method that enable numerically exact calculations at low temperatures and high spectral resolution. Key insights about the putative Planckian relaxation in the strange metal can be gained by extending the study to the frequency and time domains. Our results indicate that Planckian behaviour is rooted in the quantum statistical nature of the charge response, rather than the temperature dependence of the scattering processes they undergo. The origin of the strange metal state is still not known. Now, numerical results suggest that it follows from the quantum statistics of charge carriers, not the temperature dependence of the processes that scatter them.

title: Probing picosecond depairing currents in type-II superconductors
summary: Accessing the intrinsic critical current density in type-II superconductors can provide a means to probe microscopic superconducting properties and increase current limits in high-magnetic-field devices and electrical power systems. However, the critical current density measured using direct currents generally lies below this intrinsic limit, mainly because of vortex motion and self-heating. Here we show that picosecond electrical pulses, which act on timescales too short for vortices to move, drive supercurrents up to the intrinsic depairing limit. We probe picosecond critical currents in NbN and YBa2Cu3O7, representative s-wave and d-wave superconductors, respectively. In NbN, we find a sharp onset of the picosecond depairing at a current density of about 2.2 times the conventional critical current density, consistent with microscopic dynamics based on Bardeen–Cooper–Schrieffer theory. By contrast, YBa2Cu3O7 exhibits a gradual suppression of superconductivity with increasing current, reflecting its d-wave symmetry. These results provide a probe of superconductors beyond the reach of conventional transport measurements. Attaining the depairing current could also support superconducting electronics operating closer to intrinsic current limits. Vortex motion and heating prevent direct-current measurements from reaching the intrinsic depairing limit of type-II superconductors. Picosecond pulses bypass these effects and reveal a sharp threshold in NbN but gradual pair breaking in YBa2Cu3O7.

title: An information-theoretic proof of the Planckian bound for thermalization
summary: It has been conjectured that the speed of thermalization is universally constrained by a Planckian timescale, τPl = ℏ/(kBT), determined solely by the reduced Planck constant ℏ, Boltzmann’s constant (kB) and the temperature (T). However, a general and model-independent derivation of this limit has remained elusive. Here we provide a general proof of the emergence of Planckian thermalization based on quantum information geometry and quantum metrology. We formulate thermalization as a process that prepares states close to the corresponding thermal ensemble for a set of distinct Hamiltonians, and show that quantum mechanics imposes a universal lower bound τ ≥ τPl/2 on the thermalization time τ at finite temperature. In the low-temperature regime, the spectral gap Δ between the ground and first excited states replaces the temperature as the relevant energy scale and determines the lower bound on the thermalization time, in close connection with the quantum adiabatic theorem. These bounds, rooted in Hamiltonian estimation, establish operational limits on thermalization governed exclusively by fundamental constants and the intrinsic energy scale. Studies of many-body physics have indicated that thermalization processes are bounded by a timescale determined by Planck’s constant. Such a bound has now been proved to apply in general using techniques from quantum information theory.
